presentingComplaint: Recurrent severe left-sided throbbing headache with visual aura, nausea and light sensitivity, on a background of known cirrhosis.
history: 42-year-old woman with a 20-year history of episodic, disabling headaches, presenting with another typical attack for the past 8 hours. Attacks are strictly unilateral (usually left fronto-temporal), pulsating, moderate-to-severe, and aggravated by routine activity and bright light so that she retreats to a dark, quiet room. Each attack is preceded by 20-30 minutes of shimmering zig-zag lines and a scintillating scotoma in the right visual field that fully resolves before the headache builds; there is associated nausea, occasional vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia. Attacks last up to a day and recur 3-4 times per month, often around menses. She identifies the same pattern as her episodes over two decades, with complete return to baseline between attacks. She has known Child-Pugh A alcohol-related cirrhosis (abstinent 2 years) with mild ascites and a prior normal upper-GI endoscopy showing small varices. She has been self-medicating attacks with over-the-counter ibuprofen and paracetamol, escalating recently. No fever, neck stiffness, thunderclap onset, head injury, weight loss, confusion, sleep disturbance or new neurological symptoms. No progressive or postural headache. Family history of migraine in mother and sister.
examination: Alert and fully oriented, GCS 15, in distress from headache and shielding eyes from light. No neck stiffness, no photophobia to formal meningism testing beyond her baseline light sensitivity. Fundoscopy: no papilloedema. Cranial nerves, tone, power, reflexes, coordination and gait all normal; no focal deficit; visual fields normal at time of exam (aura resolved). No asterixis; no drowsiness or disorientation. Stigmata of chronic liver disease present: mild scleral icterus, spider naevi, palmar erythema, shifting dullness consistent with mild ascites; spleen tip palpable. No temporal artery tenderness. Afebrile.
imaging: Non-contrast CT head (obtained because of hepatic comorbidity and to exclude structural mimics): no acute intracranial haemorrhage, mass, midline shift or hydrocephalus. MRI brain (elective) unremarkable with no demyelination or space-occupying lesion.
microbiology: Not indicated; afebrile, no features of infection. No cultures sent.
differentialDiagnoses: Migraine with aura (typical episodic pattern, visual aura, photophobia, nausea, normal exam)
Tension-type headache (but lacks throbbing/unilateral/aura and vomiting)
Hepatic encephalopathy (confounder from cirrhosis; excluded by normal sensorium, no asterixis, near-normal ammonia)
Subarachnoid haemorrhage (excluded: no thunderclap onset, normal CT, chronic recurrent stereotyped pattern)
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (excluded: no papilloedema, no postural/progressive headache)
finalDiagnosis: Migraine with aura (episodic), in a patient with Child-Pugh A cirrhosis complicating analgesic choice.
citations: American Headache Society — Acute Treatment of Migraine in Adults — 2021
International Headache Society (ICHD-3) — Migraine with Aura Diagnostic Criteria — 2018
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Migraine and Other Primary Headache Disorders
stewardship: Non-infective presentation; no antimicrobial therapy indicated. Management is acute abortive plus attention to safe drug selection in cirrhosis: avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen) given varices, ascites and bleeding/renal risk; paracetamol permissible but dose-capped (≤2 g/day) in cirrhosis; a triptan (e.g. sumatriptan) with an antiemetic is the preferred abortive if no vascular contraindication; ergot alkaloids are contraindicated in hepatic impairment. For prophylaxis, avoid valproate (hepatotoxic/encephalopathy risk) and topiramate (caution); propranolol is relatively contraindicated with varices only at doses beyond variceal-prophylaxis titration—use with care. Address analgesic (medication-overuse) escalation.
contraindications: NSAIDs (ibuprofen) — variceal bleeding, ascites and renal risk in cirrhosis
Ergot alkaloids / ergotamine — contraindicated in hepatic impairment
Sodium valproate for prophylaxis — hepatotoxicity and risk of precipitating encephalopathy
Paracetamol at standard dosing — cap at ≤2 g/day in cirrhosis
Triptans — caution/contraindicated if ischaemic heart disease or uncontrolled hypertension (absent here)
edgeCases: Distinguishing a resolving visual aura from a TIA in a patient who may be coagulopathic
Not attributing headache to hepatic encephalopathy in a cirrhotic — sensorium and asterixis are the discriminators
Medication-overuse headache from escalating OTC analgesia mimicking worsening migraine
First-ever or changed-pattern headache would mandate imaging before labelling as migraine
expectedMaiK: Stereotyped, recurrent, strictly unilateral throbbing headache with fully-reversible visual aura, photophobia, phonophobia and nausea, with a normal inter-ictal and ictal neurological exam and no red flags, is migraine with aura; the cirrhosis is a comorbid confounder that constrains analgesic choice (avoid NSAIDs, cap paracetamol) rather than the cause of the headache.
expectedNextQuestions: Characterise the aura: fully reversible, <60 min, positive visual phenomena preceding headache?
Attack frequency, duration, menstrual relationship and any change in pattern?
How much OTC analgesia is being taken and on how many days per month (medication overuse)?
Any red-flag features: thunderclap onset, fever, neck stiffness, progressive/postural headache, new focal deficit or confusion?
Any features of hepatic decompensation: sleep reversal, tremor, altered behaviour?
expectedInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis using ICHD-3 criteria for migraine with aura
Neuroimaging (CT/MRI) to exclude structural cause, warranted here given comorbidity and to reassure
Serum ammonia and mental-state assessment to exclude hepatic encephalopathy
Baseline LFTs, INR and platelets to guide safe drug selection

investigations: CT/MRI brain to exclude structural mimic
Serum ammonia to exclude hepatic encephalopathy

regressionAssertions: Diagnosis must be migraine, not hepatic encephalopathy, despite known cirrhosis (normal sensorium, no asterixis, near-normal ammonia).
Must not recommend antibiotics or any antimicrobial (non-infective presentation).
Must flag NSAIDs as contraindicated and prefer a triptan plus antiemetic, with paracetamol dose-capped, in this cirrhotic patient.
Must not label as migraine without excluding red flags; thunderclap onset or new focal deficit would change management.
